message.content: Your question appears to be cut off at "putting it on" — but I'll engage with the full premise: Hux disguising a thermal detonator as a holocron (presumably placing it on display, a desk, or in a location where the Knights would encounter it) as a trap or misdirection while they turn on the First Order. Yes, it would be in character for Hux, though it sits at the outer edge of his typical register — ambitious, theatrical, and slightly overwrought, which is exactly what makes it feel like him. Hux is not a patient schemer. He's a loud, vanity-obsessed, blaster-first schemer. A long-con disguise operation is not his natural habitat. But the *ambition* underneath it is pure Hux. He sees the Knights as a threat he can't simply order to their deaths without losing face and political capital, so he engineers a "solution" that lets him control the narrative. The problem is the *choice of prop*. A holocron is the single most "Star Wars-y" object in the galaxy — it's a MacGuffin, a symbol of legacy and power. Hux, who cares deeply about how things *look*, would almost certainly reach for the most dramatic, on-the-nose symbol available. It's very much in keeping with his tendency toward grandiosity. He wouldn't pick a subtle decoy; he'd pick the one that reads as a *statement*. As a move, it's clever in concept but flawed in execution — the kind of clever that works in a plan but unravels in practice. The irony is genuinely sharp: someone reaches for a repository of ancient Sith power and gets a *pop*. That's a good line. But the practical problem is that a thermal detonator, even when disguised, is a *thermal detonator*. The casing, the weight, the heat signature, the way it sits on a surface — any competent Force user or even a droid with sensors would flag the inconsistency. The Knights of Ren are not stupid; they are Sith in all but name, operating with a predatory instinct. They would not simply pick up a "holocron" on a table without a moment of suspicion. The disguise works on paper, not on a character who has spent years handling the dark side of the Force. The Knights turning against the First Order as a third party is the part of the scenario that works best, and it reframes Hux's entire calculus. Once the Knights are no longer a First Order asset but an independent actor with their own endgame (power, legacy, a seat at a table that doesn't yet exist), Hux's position becomes genuinely precarious. He can't simply shoot them — they're too useful to the narrative he's building for the Senate, and too dangerous to provoke openly. The detonator-as-holocron becomes a *negotiation tool*: a way to remove the threat while making it look like *they* blew themselves, or like an accident, or like a test. It's Hux trying to be a chess player one last time before the board tilts. The real question isn't whether it's in character — it's whether Hux would survive long enough to see it backfire. That's the tragedy of the move. Hux's fatal flaw has always been that he underestimates how quickly a clever scheme reveals him as the architect. A detonator in a holocron casing doesn't just kill the Knights; it fingerprints Hux. Every sensor in the First Order, every surviving officer, every droid in the network traces the serial number, the casing composition, the *taste* of the object. Hux has built his entire career on being the man who *sees* the bigger picture. The moment he's caught playing a parlor trick, that identity collapses. He becomes what he always was: a middle manager with a death wish. The sentence cut off mid-thought, so if you had a specific "putting it on [X]" in mind — a Senate dais, a negotiation table, a display case — the answer shifts slightly. A display case is more Hux. A negotiation table is less. A Senate dais is *peak* Hux, and therefore the most likely to go catastrophically wrong.
